task: Published numerical values of the Jacobi constant at the Earth-Moon CR3BP libration points L1-L5, with each source's mass ratio mu and the exact C definition used. External anchor set for a numerical experiment.

B_Omega_includes_mu(1-mu)/2.Omega: Omega = 0.5*(x^2+y^2) + (1-mu)/r1 + mu/r2 + 0.5*mu*(1-mu)   (= Szebehely's pseudo-potential; equivalently Omega = 0.5*[(1-mu)*r1^2 + mu*r2^2] + (1-mu)/r1 + mu/r2)
B_Omega_includes_mu(1-mu)/2.C: C = 2*Omega - v^2  =>  C_B = C_A + mu*(1-mu)  (a pure constant offset)
B_Omega_includes_mu(1-mu)/2.C_L4_L5: C_L4 = C_L5 = 3 exactly, independent of mu

sources.name: Isolating blocks as computational tools in the circular restricted three-body problem (AAS 15-615; journal version: Physica D 343:38-50)
sources.authors: Rodney L. Anderson, Robert W. Easton, Martin W. Lo
sources.mu_statement: stated verbatim: 'The mass parameter for the Earth-Moon system used here mu is = 1.2150584270571545x10^-2'
sources.definition: Phi(x,y,z) = 0.5*(x^2+y^2) + U(x,y,z), U = lambda/rho1 + mu/rho2 with lambda = 1-mu; J = 0.5*<qdot,qdot> - Phi(q); J = -C/2, i.e. C = 2*Phi(q) - <qdot,qdot> = x^2+y^2 + 2*(1-mu)/rho1 + 2*mu/rho2 - (xdot^2+ydot^2+zdot^2)
sources.evidence_quote: 'The mass parameter for the Earth-Moon system used here mu is = 1.2150584270571545x10^-2.' (p.2) | 'Phi(x,y,z) = 1/2 (x^2+y^2) + U(x,y,z) ... U(x,y,z) = lambda/rho1(x,y,z) + mu/rho2(x,y,z)' (p.2) | 'The Jacobi Integral J = 1/2 <qdot,qdot> - Phi(q) is a constant of motion for this model, and the Jacobi constant is defined by the equation J = -C/2.' (p.2) | 'As a reference, the Jacobi constants computed at each libration point in the Earth-Moon system are CL1 = 3.1883411054012485 CL2 = 3.1721604503998044 CL3 = 3.0121471493422489 CL4 = CL5 = 2.9879970524275450.' (p.3)
sources.evidence_location: pp. 2-3 of the AAS 15-615 preprint PDF
sources.verification_method: PDF downloaded to tests/_anchor_sources/aas15-615.pdf and read with a PDF reader; all four C values independently reproduced to 15-16 significant digits from the paper's own mu and definition (mpmath, 40 digits).
sources.caveats: Conference preprint AAS 15-615; the journal version is Physica D 343 (2017) 38-50.
sources.note_on_numeric_field: The numeric C field below is float64 and rounds L3 to 3.012147149342249; use C_exact_as_published for the verbatim 16-digit strings.

sources.name: Nomology of Earth-Moon Orbits, C = 4.00 and C = C(L1) (NASA TN D-5949)
sources.authors: R. F. Hoelker (NASA Electronics Research Center)
sources.mu_statement: report states 'The ratio of the masses is 1:79' and 'a mass ratio mu of 1/80'; with mu = m2/(m1+m2) this is mu = 0.0125 exactly. Independently confirmed: the report's L1 position XR(L1) = 0.8352093934 is reproduced to 11 digits by mu = 0.0125.
sources.definition: The report's Jacobi integral equation (Eq. 5) is not legible in the OCR, but its quoted C-levels are only reproducible with the constant-included convention: C = 2*Omega - v^2 with Omega = 0.5*(x^2+y^2) + (1-mu)/r1 + mu/r2 + 0.5*mu*(1-mu). (With mu = 0.0125 the same points give C_L1 = 3.191542 without the constant, far from the quoted 3.20388.)
sources.evidence_quote: 'The mathematical representation of the problem is done by the restricted problem of three bodies with a mass ratio mu of 1/80.' (Summary) | 'The ratio of the masses is 1:79 ...' (p.3) | 'The overall appearance of these "zero-velocity-curves" is depicted in Figure 2, for the C-values of 3.30; 3.20388; 3.18720; 3.10; 3.02484; 3.010 and 3.0010.' (p.5) | 'With decrease of the Jacobian constant to C = 3.20388 the terrestrial and lunar regions increase such that they touch each other (see Figure 4). The point of tangency is marked as L1' (p.5) | 'Figure 7 then illustrates the point of C-curve development at which the third gate at L3 starts to open. The corresponding C-value is C = 3.02484.' (p.6) | 'for a value of C = 3.00 these two parts degenerate to a single point each (L4 and L5), which are equilateral to the masses. These two points represent the only stable ones of the five equilibrium points.' (Summary)
sources.verification_method: PDF downloaded from NTRS and read; C(L1) and C(L3) independently reproduced (3.203886 and 3.024840) from mu = 0.0125 under convention B; L1 position reproduced exactly.
sources.caveats: The quoted C(L2) = 3.18720 differs by 4.1e-5 from the value recomputed here (3.1872413) - probably a typo/rounding in the 1970 report. The report is a pictorial atlas: L1/L2/L3 values are read from the text describing the zero-velocity-curve gates, not from a C table.

sources.name: Order-chaos-order and invariant manifolds in the bounded planar Earth-Moon system (Celest. Mech. Dyn. Astron. 132:51)
sources.authors: V. M. de Oliveira, P. A. Sousa-Silva, I. L. Caldas
sources.definition: Omega = 0.5*(x^2+y^2) + (1-mu)/r1 + mu/r2; C = 2*Omega - xdot^2 - ydot^2. No mu(1-mu)/2 term.
sources.evidence_quote: 'For the Earth-Moon system, we have mu = 1.2150 x 10^-2.' | 'Omega = 1/2(x^2 + y^2) + (1-mu)/sqrt((x+mu)^2+y^2) + mu/sqrt((x-(1-mu))^2+y^2)' and 'C = 2Omega - xdot^2 - ydot^2' | 'C1 ~ 3.1883 and C2 ~ 3.1722 are the Jacobi constants at the Lagrangian points L1 and L2, respectively.'
sources.evidence_location: full text (ar5iv HTML of arXiv:2006.13111); values quoted in Sec. 2 and the Fig. 1 discussion
sources.verification_method: ar5iv HTML full text opened and read; only L1 and L2 values are published (no L3-L5).
sources.caveats: mu given to 4 significant figures only; C values to 4 decimal places. Independent corroboration of the 3.1883 / 3.1722 pair.

sources.name: Low-Thrust Earth-Moon Transfer Trajectories to Stable Distant Retrograde Orbits using Indirect Optimization Method (MSc thesis, Politecnico di Torino)
sources.mu_statement: No explicit mu value found in the sections read. mu is IMPLIED by Table 2.2 itself: L4 xi = 0.48785136 = 0.5 - mu => mu = 0.01214864; the C values are consistent with mu = 0.0121485 (C_L4 = 3 - mu + mu^2 = 2.987999). Its Table 2.1 GM values (Earth 3.9860e5, Moon 4.9028e3) would instead give mu = 0.0121506 - a ~2e-6 internal inconsistency.
sources.verification_method: PDF downloaded and read; C values and the L3/L4/L5 coordinates independently reproduced from mu = 0.01214864.
sources.caveats: The L1 and L2 x-coordinates printed in Table 2.2 (0.83740242, 1.15618808) are NOT consistent with its own C values: they imply mu ~ 0.01205, whereas C_L4 = 2.987999 and L4 x = 0.48785136 imply mu ~ 0.0121486. Treat the C column (not the L1/L2 x column) as the anchor. mu is inferred, not stated.

(p.16)

sources.evidence_quote: '6.4 Jacobi Constant. In the CR3BP, there exists a constant of motion commonly labeled the Jacobi constant C_J, written as a function of the nondimensional state vector and mass ratio as: C_J = (x^2 + y^2) + 2(1-mu)/r1 + 2mu/r2 - xdot^2 - ydot^2 - zdot^2 (112)' (report p.71; PDF p.76). derived_values_not_published.warning: These numbers were computed by me from the definitions verified in the opened sources (conventions A and B above). They are NOT published values and must not be cited as literature anchors; they are given only to quantify how much mu and the convention shift the C values.

shift_between_conventions.formula: C_B - C_A = mu*(1-mu) for every L point (a pure constant offset)

notes: SUMMARY AND DIFFERENCES. (1) Two conventions dominate. Convention A (Omega = 0.5(x^2+y^2)+(1-mu)/r1+mu/r2, C = 2*Omega - v^2) gives C_L4 = C_L5 = 3 - mu + mu^2 (about 2.9880 for Earth-Moon) and is used by AAS 15-615/Physica D, Gupta 2020, de Oliveira 2020, Pice 2024, NASA/TP-20220014814 and (by its numbers) the JPL DESCANSO volume. Convention B (Omega additionally contains +0.5*mu*(1-mu), i.e. Szebehely's pseudo-potential) shifts every C by exactly +mu*(1-mu) and makes C_L4 = C_L5 = 3 exactly; it is used by Hoelker 1971 (NASA TN D-5949), the ESA/ARI 2004 report, the CMES 2023 review and the Majer thesis. The convention offset (~0.0120 for the modern Earth-Moon mu, ~0.0123 for mu = 0.0125) is roughly 100x larger than any mu-induced difference - always record the convention. (2) mu values actually used by the verified sources: 0.012150584270571545 (AAS 15-615, 16 digits); 0.0121506 (Gupta 2020); 0.0121500 (de Oliveira 2020, 4 s.f.); ~0.0121486 implied (Pice 2024); 0.01214 (CMES 2023, rounded); 0.0121409319 (ESA/ARI 2004); 0.0125 = 1/80 (Hoelker 1971). The commonly quoted 0.0121505856 and 0.012277471 are NOT the mu of any of the verified numerical tables: 0.0121505856 reproduces the AAS/Gupta values to ~1e-7, while 0.012277471 is the classical Arenstorf test-problem value and would shift C_L1 by +1.17e-3 and C_L4 by -1.24e-4 (convention A). (3) Effect of mu on the anchor values (convention A): C_L4 = 3-mu+mu^2 is 2.9879971 (mu = 0.0121506), 2.9879990 (mu = 0.0121486), 2.9880065 (mu = 0.0121409319), 2.9878733 (mu = 0.012277471) and 2.9876563 (mu = 0.0125) - i.e. the 4th-5th decimal moves. (4) Rounding/typo-level differences among sources: AAS 15-615 vs Gupta 2020 agree to 5 dp; JPL DESCANSO's 8-digit values are ~1.5e-7 above AAS's 16-digit values and are internally inconsistent with its own L4 coordinate (which implies mu = 0.0121505843) at the 8th decimal; Hoelker's C(L2) = 3.18720 is 4.1e-5 below the recomputed 3.1872413 (likely a typo); the Pice thesis's L1/L2 x-coordinates are inconsistent with its own C values; the CMES review quotes C_L1 = 3.2003 while stating mu = 0.01214 (that value matches mu ~ 0.01215). (5) RECOMMENDED ANCHOR for a numerical experiment: use S1 (AAS 15-615) as the primary anchor because it states mu to 16 digits, states its definition unambiguously, and its four C values were independently reproduced here to 15-16 significant digits; cross-check with S2 (Gupta 2020) and, if a NASA/JPL anchor is required, with U1 (JPL DESCANSO Table 2-4) - noting that U1 is index-read only. If the experiment uses mu = 0.012277471 (Szebehely/Arenstorf), there is no published L1-L5 C table for that mu that I could verify; use the derived values above and say explicitly that they are computed, not published. (6) Do not mix sources across conventions without shifting by mu*(1-mu).
